headline: The Sensex rose 383 points to 77,301 for a fifth straight gain as smaller companies and media shares led after Democrats won the US Congress; BEL jumped 4.71%, IT shares fell, and the rupee gained 17 paise to 94.58.
mood_note: A calmer but broad rise: most shares gained, with smaller companies doing best. IT was the only weak sector. Investors welcomed the US election result, and oil eased further.
since_yesterday: On Tuesday we reported Brent crude at $105.46 at about 3:36 pm. It ended the day 1.1% lower, settling at $103.60, according to news reports.
We reported the rupee at 94.71 per dollar (provisional) on Tuesday. The final figure was 94.75, according to news reports.
Exchange data showed foreign institutional investors bought Indian shares worth about ₹6,837 crore, net, on Tuesday, while domestic institutions sold about ₹3,679 crore.
one_minute: The Sensex rose 383.55 points (0.50%) to 77,301.40 and the Nifty 50 rose 149.75 points (0.63%) to 23,960.60, a fifth straight gain. The Nifty Smallcap 100 jumped 2%.
Democrats won control of both houses of the US Congress, according to US network projections. US stock futures jumped, US bond yields fell, and gold rose.
Bharat Electronics rose 4.71%, the top Nifty gainer, after sticking to its target of ₹55,000 crore in new defence orders this year; IT shares such as TCS fell.
The rupee rose 17 paise to 94.58 per dollar (provisional) as Brent crude slipped to about $101.85.
The RBI formed an expert panel on bond, currency and derivatives markets, and said a viral circular about a shortage of small notes is fake.
big_picture:
Indian shares rose for a fifth day in a row on Wednesday. The jump was smaller than earlier this week, but it was broad, and smaller companies did best.

The main news came from America. In Tuesday's midterm elections, the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress, according to US network projections. That means President Trump will need the other party's support for new laws. Many investors saw this as a sign of fewer sudden policy shocks, such as surprise trade taxes, and markets around the world cheered.

India's IT companies, which earn much of their money in the US, were the exception and fell.

Oil slipped again, to about $102 a barrel, and the rupee strengthened. Gold jumped, just two days before Dhanteras.

Over five days, the Sensex has gained more than 4,000 points. That is a strong run, but markets rarely move in a straight line.

stories.title: Sensex rises 383 points for a fifth straight gain, as smaller companies and media shares lead and IT lags
stories.tldr: The Sensex rose 383.55 points, or 0.50%, to 77,301.40, and the Nifty 50 rose 149.75 points, or 0.63%, to 23,960.60, a fifth straight gain. Smaller companies did even better: the Nifty Smallcap 100 jumped 2%. Media shares rose more than 5%, while IT was the only sector to fall.
stories.what_happened:
The Sensex rose 383.55 points, or 0.50%, to 77,301.40, and the Nifty 50 rose 149.75 points, or 0.63%, to 23,960.60, ANI and Zee Business reported. It was the fifth day of gains in a row, and the Nifty's highest close in about two months, 5paisa said. Over the five sessions the Sensex has gained 4,055 points and the Nifty 1,261.75 points, and investors' shares have risen about ₹20.8 lakh crore in value, BusinessToday reported.

Smaller companies did better than the big ones. The Nifty Midcap 100 rose 1.55% to 59,505.50 and the Nifty Smallcap 100 jumped 2% to 19,026.40. Of the 50 Nifty shares, 36 rose and 14 fell.

The Nifty Media index jumped 5.15%, the best sector, followed by Realty (about 2.8%) and Metal (2.40%). Nifty IT was the only sector to fall, by between 1.50% and 1.94% depending on the report. Bharat Electronics (BEL) rose 4.71%, Adani Enterprises about 4.47% and Titan about 4.22%; TCS fell 2.52% and HCL Tech 2.37%. India VIX, the 'fear gauge', fell 3.44% to 15.23, HDFC Sky reported.
stories.simple_explanation:
Indian shares rose for a fifth day in a row. The gain was smaller than on Monday and Tuesday, about half a percent, but it was very broad.

The biggest winners were smaller and medium-sized companies, which rose two to three times as much as the big ones. Media companies, such as TV broadcasters, had a very strong day, and so did property and metal firms.

The one weak spot was IT companies like TCS and Infosys. Everything else rose.

Many investors felt relieved after the US election result, which came in today, India time. That is our second story.
stories.analogy: It is like a school sports day where the big stars only jog, but the junior teams sprint ahead. The overall score still goes up, and more students take home medals.
stories.why:
Vinod Nair of Geojit Investments linked the gains partly to the US midterm election result, which raised hopes of a more measured US approach to trade and tariffs, BusinessToday reported. That could help foreign investors put more money into countries like India. He also pointed to hopes of tax relief in the next Union Budget, better-than-expected company results and strong festive shopping. 5paisa credited falling crude prices and continued buying by foreign investors.

Foreign institutional investors bought shares worth about ₹6,837 crore, net, on Tuesday, while domestic institutions sold about ₹3,679 crore, according to provisional exchange data.

We did not find a clear reason for the jump in media shares; reports described strong buying in TV broadcasters such as Zee Entertainment.

implications.you: If you hold a Nifty 50 index fund or an equity mutual fund through a SIP, it has probably gained over the past week. Small-cap funds probably did even better today. Five good days don't tell you anything about the next five.
implications.markets: When smaller companies rise more than big ones and most shares go up, traders usually see it as a sign of confidence. But after a gain of more than 5% in a week, some investors may sell to lock in profits.
implications.economy: No direct effect on the economy today. Analysts did mention strong festive shopping, a sign that people are spending.
implications.prices: No direct effect on everyday prices today.

stories.watch: Whether foreign investors keep buying, how oil moves as US-Iran talks continue, and Titan's results, due on Thursday.

explainers.like12:
Imagine your class has had five tests this week, and the class average went up every time. Today it went up only a little, but almost everyone improved, especially the students who usually sit in the middle and back rows.

The Sensex and Nifty are numbers that follow India's biggest companies. They rose again today, for the fifth day running. Smaller companies did even better than the giants.

Companies that run TV channels had a great day. The only group that slipped was computer-software companies, like TCS.

One reason people felt cheerful: an election in America finished in a way many investors liked, because it might make sudden trade fights less likely. When people feel calmer, they buy more shares.
explainers.real_life:
Meet Kavya, a 27-year-old nurse in Kochi. Two years ago she started a ₹2,000 monthly SIP in a small-cap fund, and another ₹2,000 in a Nifty 50 index fund.

This week, both funds have gained, and today her small-cap fund probably did better because smaller companies jumped 2%. It is tempting for her to move all her money into the small-cap fund.

But small-cap funds also fall much harder in bad weeks. Just two weeks ago, the Nifty Smallcap 100 had fallen more than 7% in a single week. Kavya's split between the two funds is meant to balance that risk. A good week is a nice moment to check her plan, but not a reason to change it on the spot.

stories.title: Democrats win control of the US Congress; US stock futures jump, bond yields fall and gold rises
stories.tldr: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the US midterm elections, according to projections by US news networks, though some races were still being counted. US stock futures rose sharply, US bond yields and the dollar fell, and gold jumped. India's IT shares fell.
stories.what_happened:
Democrats won control of both houses of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, CNN and CBS News projected. CNN projected that the party had won at least 51 seats in the 100-seat Senate. Many House races were still being counted on Wednesday. President Donald Trump told the New York Times he was willing to accept the results, CNBC reported.

US stock futures, which point to how Wall Street may open, first fell overnight and then jumped. Futures tied to the Dow Jones rose 912 points, or 1.75%, CNBC reported. The US 10-year Treasury yield fell 6 basis points to 4.906%, and the dollar weakened, according to market reports.

Gold rose too. Spot gold was up 2.4% at $4,021.68 an ounce at 12:48 pm India time, Reuters reported, and December gold on MCX was at ₹1,41,957 per 10 grams around midday, up about 1.8%, according to NDTV Profit. Dhanteras is on Friday, 6 November.
stories.simple_explanation:
America held an important election on Tuesday. Voters chose many members of their parliament, called Congress. The President's opponents, the Democrats, won control of both parts of it.

This means President Trump will need the other party's agreement to pass new laws. Many investors like that, because it makes sudden big policy changes, such as new trade taxes, less likely.

After the result, investors expected US shares to rise, and interest rates on US government bonds fell. Gold also jumped, just before Dhanteras.

In India, the news helped the overall mood, though IT companies, which earn much of their money in America, fell.
stories.analogy: It is like a family where one parent wanted to make big changes to the house. Now the other parent has to sign off on every plan. Fewer surprises, slower decisions.
stories.why:
Markets generally prefer power in Washington to be split between the two parties, because it lowers the risk of sweeping policy changes, AP reported. CNN said hopes that the result would limit heavy government borrowing and spending pushed bond yields lower. Some investors had also feared a long fight over the results; Trump's acceptance eased that worry, CNBC said.

Gold rose because of a weaker dollar and lower US bond yields after the election, Reuters reported. Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar tends to lift it.

One report, by HDFC Sky, linked the fall in Indian IT shares to worries about what the result could mean for US technology spending. We found only one source for that explanation.

implications.you: If you plan to buy gold for Dhanteras, it was more expensive today than on Tuesday. Shop prices also include GST and making charges. Gold prices move every day and are hard to predict.
implications.markets: Lower US bond yields and a weaker dollar can make countries like India more attractive to foreign investors, analysts say. Results in some US races are still coming in, and markets may react further.
implications.economy: If the US moves to calmer trade policies, Indian exporters could benefit, but no actual policy has changed yet.
implications.prices: No direct effect on everyday prices yet. A weaker dollar can help the rupee, which makes imports slightly cheaper.

stories.watch: How Wall Street closes on Wednesday night, India time, and the final count of US House seats.

explainers.like12:
Imagine your school has a head teacher and a student council. The head teacher can suggest new rules, but the council has to agree before they start. Until now, most of the council was on the head teacher's side. In yesterday's vote, the other side won the council.

That's what happened in America. The US President's party lost control of Congress, which makes the country's laws.

Why do investors care? Many think it means fewer sudden surprises, like new taxes on goods from other countries, because the President now needs the other side to agree. People who invest money usually like fewer surprises.

Gold also became more expensive today, which matters in India because many families buy gold at Dhanteras, this Friday.
explainers.real_life:
Meet Suresh, a 35-year-old software tester in Pune. His company does most of its work for American clients.

Today, IT shares like TCS and Infosys fell, while most other shares rose. Suresh wonders if the US election will hurt his job. The honest answer: nothing has changed yet. No new law has passed, and his company's contracts are the same as yesterday. Share prices moved on guesses about the future, not on actual decisions.

Suresh's wife, Anjali, had planned to buy a gold coin for Dhanteras on Friday. Gold rose sharply today, so the same coin costs a bit more than it did on Tuesday. Prices could move either way by Friday, so she decides to stick to her budget rather than chase the price.

stories.title: Bharat Electronics rises 4.71%, the top Nifty gainer, as it sticks to its target for new defence orders
stories.tldr: Shares of Bharat Electronics (BEL), a government-owned defence company, rose 4.71% to ₹398, the best performance among Nifty 50 shares. Its July–September profit rose about 20% to ₹1,540.37 crore. BEL kept its target of winning ₹55,000 crore of new orders this year, even though orders won last quarter fell.
stories.what_happened:
BEL shares rose 4.71% to ₹398.00 on the NSE, making it the top Nifty 50 gainer, Angel One reported. About 2.35 crore BEL shares changed hands, IndiaInfoline said.

In its results for July–September, BEL's consolidated profit rose 19.68% to ₹1,540.37 crore, the Free Press Journal reported. Its revenue from operations rose 26.49% to about ₹7,291 crore, according to Kotak Neo. Profit grew more slowly than revenue, a sign of some pressure on margins.

BEL repeated its target of winning ₹55,000 crore of new orders in the 2026-27 financial year, even though orders won in the July–September quarter fell 31%, Business Standard reported. Analysts at Motilal Oswal raised their target price for the share to ₹540 from ₹530.

The share had touched a 52-week low of ₹354.55 on 23 October, Zee Business reported.
stories.simple_explanation:
Bharat Electronics, or BEL, makes radars, missile systems and electronics for India's armed forces. The government owns most of it.

Its profit for July to September rose about a fifth from a year ago, and its sales rose about a quarter.

But investors care most about how many new orders BEL wins, because those become future sales. New orders last quarter were lower. Still, BEL said it expects a big jump in new orders over the rest of the year, and investors believed it. Its shares rose almost 5%, the most among India's 50 biggest companies today.
stories.analogy: It is like a tailor whose shop had a quiet month for new bookings, but who tells you the wedding season rush is coming. If customers trust the tailor's past record, they believe the promise.
stories.why:
Investors were encouraged that BEL kept its full-year order target despite a weak quarter for new orders, Business Standard reported, and brokerages including Motilal Oswal stayed positive on the company. Defence companies' future earnings depend heavily on the orders they win from the government, so a confident order outlook matters more to investors than one quarter's profit.

The share had also fallen to its lowest level in a year in late October, which may have made it look cheaper to some buyers.

implications.you: If you own an index fund or a mutual fund that holds large Indian companies, it probably holds a little BEL. One share's move has only a small effect on your fund.
implications.markets: BEL's order target will be tested over the next five months. If big orders don't arrive, investors may become less patient.
implications.economy: Large defence orders to Indian companies support factories and jobs in India, including at smaller suppliers.

stories.watch: Whether BEL announces large new defence contracts in the coming months.

explainers.like12:
Imagine a company that makes the special electronic eyes and ears for India's army, navy and air force: radars that spot planes, systems that guide missiles. That's Bharat Electronics, or BEL.

BEL gets most of its work as big orders from the government. Each order can take years to finish. So people who own BEL shares watch two things: how much money it made, and how many new orders it won.

This time, BEL made more money than last year. New orders were lower for a few months, but BEL promised that many more are coming before March. People believed it, and BEL's share price went up almost 5%, more than any other big company today.
explainers.real_life:
Meet Prakash, a 40-year-old electrician in Bengaluru. He works for a small firm that makes cable parts and sells some of them to BEL.

For Prakash, today's share price jump doesn't change his pay. What matters more is BEL's promise of ₹55,000 crore in new orders this year. If those orders arrive, BEL will buy more parts from suppliers like his employer, which could mean steady work and perhaps overtime.

If Prakash owns a mutual fund through a SIP, it may hold a small amount of BEL. But his fund owns dozens of companies, so one share's 4.71% rise barely shows up in his statement. His real link to BEL is through his job, not his investments.

stories.title: Rupee gains 17 paise to 94.58 as oil slips to about $102 and the dollar weakens
stories.tldr: The rupee rose 17 paise to 94.58 against the US dollar (provisional), its second straight gain. Brent crude fell to about $101.85 a barrel, down 0.7%, as traders weighed the US election result and uncertain US-Iran talks. Foreign investors' buying of Indian shares also helped the rupee.
stories.what_happened:
The rupee settled 17 paise higher at 94.58 against the US dollar (provisional), its second straight gain, news reports said. It had touched 94.50 during the day. Easing crude prices, a weaker dollar and money coming in from foreign investors supported it.

Brent crude, the international oil price, fell $1.75, or 0.7%, to $101.85 a barrel by 4:04 pm India time, after falling $2 earlier in the day, news reports said. On Tuesday it had settled at $103.60.

Traders were weighing the US election result and the state of US-Iran talks. Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that Tehran would not accept diplomacy based on coercion. Neil Shearing, chief economist at Capital Economics, warned that strikes on Iran could push Brent above $120.
stories.simple_explanation:
The rupee got a little stronger today. One US dollar now costs about ₹94.58, down from about ₹94.75 on Tuesday.

Three things helped. Oil got cheaper, so India needs fewer dollars to pay for it. The dollar itself weakened around the world after the US election. And foreign investors kept bringing dollars into India to buy Indian shares.

Oil has fallen from above $110 last week to about $102 because America and Iran have been talking about ending their conflict. But nobody knows if the talks will work, so oil prices are still jumpy.
stories.analogy: It is like a family whose monthly petrol bill shrinks just as a relative abroad sends money home. With less going out and more coming in, the household budget breathes easier.
stories.why:
India buys most of its oil from abroad and pays in dollars, so cheaper oil means fewer dollars are needed. A weaker US dollar after the election also helped the rupee, as did buying by foreign investors, who must change dollars into rupees to buy Indian shares.

Oil fell as traders hoped the US and Iran might reach a deal, though Iran's comments on Tuesday showed the talks are far from settled.

implications.you: If you pay for anything priced in dollars, such as a child's fees abroad or online subscriptions, today's move makes it very slightly cheaper. A 17-paise change is about 0.2%, so the effect is small.
implications.markets: A steadier rupee and cheaper oil tend to encourage foreign investors and help companies that import raw materials, such as paint and airline companies.
implications.economy: If oil stays near $100 or lower, India's import bill shrinks, which can ease pressure on the rupee and on inflation.
implications.prices: Petrol and diesel prices in India don't change daily with Brent, so there is no immediate change at the pump.

stories.watch: News from the US-Iran talks, which is the biggest swing factor for oil prices.

explainers.like12:
Imagine you want to buy a toy from a shop in America. You have to pay in dollars, so first you swap your rupees for dollars. Today, one dollar cost about ₹94.58, a little less than yesterday. So the rupee got slightly stronger.

Why? India buys a lot of oil from other countries and has to pay in dollars. Oil got a bit cheaper today, so India needs fewer dollars. Also, people from other countries are bringing dollars into India to buy shares of Indian companies.

Oil is cheaper than last week because America and Iran, which have been fighting, are talking about peace. But they haven't agreed yet, so oil prices still jump up and down a lot.
explainers.real_life:
Meet Farah, a 29-year-old accountant in Hyderabad. Her younger brother is studying in the US, and she sends him $500 every month.

At Tuesday's rate of about ₹94.75, that cost her about ₹47,375. At today's 94.58, it costs about ₹47,290, roughly ₹85 less. That is small, but such moves add up over a year, and they can also go the other way.

Farah also drives a scooter to work. Cheaper oil doesn't change petrol prices at her pump right away, because Indian fuel prices are not changed daily. But if oil stays lower for months, it can help keep inflation down, which matters for her household budget and, in time, interest rates on loans.

stories.title: RBI sets up an expert panel on bond, currency and derivatives markets, and says a viral note-shortage circular is fake
stories.tldr: The RBI formed a Technical Consultative Committee for Financial Markets, with seven outside experts, including Morgan Stanley India's Ridham Desai and former SEBI member Ananth Narayan. Separately, the RBI said a viral circular claiming ₹10, ₹20 and ₹50 notes could run short this Diwali was forged.
stories.what_happened:
The RBI set up a Technical Consultative Committee for Financial Markets with seven outside experts, BusinessToday reported. Members include Ridham Desai of Morgan Stanley India, Ananth Narayan, a former whole-time member of SEBI, Shamsher Singh of SBI, Neeraj Gambhir of Axis Bank and Shailendra Jhingan of ICICI Bank.

The committee will be chaired by the RBI Deputy Governor in charge of its financial markets regulation department. It will cover money markets, government securities, foreign exchange markets, derivatives and related market systems. The RBI had outlined the plan in a policy statement on 7 October.

Separately, the RBI dismissed viral claims that ₹10, ₹20 and ₹50 notes could run short during Diwali, calling the circular forged, BusinessToday reported.
stories.simple_explanation:
The RBI, India's central bank, looks after markets where banks and big investors borrow, lend and trade money: government bonds, short-term loans and currencies like the dollar.

Today it formed a group of experts from banks and the markets to advise it on these areas. Think of it as a panel of experienced advisers the RBI can consult before it changes rules.

In a separate update, the RBI warned that a message going around, claiming small currency notes would run short this Diwali, is fake. It never issued that circular.
stories.analogy: It is like a school principal forming a committee of senior teachers and parents to advise on exam rules, while also telling everyone that a WhatsApp message announcing an extra holiday is fake.
stories.why:
The RBI said in October that it wanted to set up such a committee. Markets for bonds, currencies and derivatives have grown large and complex, and regulators often seek advice from people who work in them before changing rules.

Fake circulars spread quickly on social media, especially around festivals, so the RBI regularly flags forged documents to stop panic.

implications.you: No direct effect on you today. The new committee may shape future rules for bond and currency markets, which can, over time, affect interest rates on loans and deposits. There is no shortage of small notes, according to the RBI.
implications.markets: Bond and currency traders will watch for any new rules that come out of the committee's advice.

stories.watch: Whether the RBI proposes changes to bond or currency market rules after consulting the new committee.

explainers.like12:
The RBI is like India's money manager. It looks after banks, prints our currency notes and keeps an eye on places where big amounts of money are lent and traded.

Today it picked seven experienced people from banks and big investment firms to give it advice. They will help the RBI think about markets where the government borrows money, where banks lend to each other for a few days, and where rupees are swapped for dollars.

The RBI also cleared up a rumour. A message going around on phones said ₹10, ₹20 and ₹50 notes would be hard to find this Diwali. The RBI said that message is fake. So if someone forwards it to your family, you can tell them it isn't true.
explainers.real_life:
Meet Geeta, a 52-year-old shopkeeper in Lucknow who runs a sweets shop. Diwali is her busiest week, and she needs lots of ₹10, ₹20 and ₹50 notes to give change.

On Tuesday, a relative forwarded her a 'circular' on WhatsApp saying small notes would run short. She almost withdrew extra cash early to be safe. Today the RBI said that circular is forged.

The lesson for Geeta: official RBI notices appear on the RBI's own website and in news reports. A forwarded image, however official it looks, should be checked first. The new RBI expert committee won't affect her shop directly, but its advice may shape bond and currency rules that, over time, influence the interest on her shop's loan.

concept.explanation:
An order book is the total value of work a company has signed contracts for but not yet delivered. It matters most for companies that work on big, long projects, such as defence makers, builders of roads and power plants, and engineering firms.

Two related numbers appear in the news. The order book is the stock of work waiting to be done. Order inflow is the value of new contracts won in a period, like a quarter. Revenue is what the company earns as it delivers that work.

A large order book gives a company years of visible future sales. But if new orders slow down, the book shrinks as old work is completed, and future sales may suffer. That is why investors often care more about order inflow and the company's order targets than about one quarter's profit.
concept.example: Bharat Electronics' new orders fell 31% in July–September, but it stuck to its target of winning ₹55,000 crore of orders in 2026-27, Business Standard reported. Its shares rose 4.71% on Wednesday.
concept.takeaway: For project-based companies, the orders they win today are the sales of tomorrow, so investors watch order inflow closely.

quiz.q: How did the Sensex end on Wednesday?
quiz.why: The Sensex rose 383.55 points, or 0.50%, to 77,301.40, its fifth straight gain. The 1,225-point rise was Tuesday's.

quiz.q: Which group of shares did best today?
options: Smaller companies, with the Nifty Smallcap 100 up 2%
quiz.why: The Nifty Smallcap 100 jumped 2% and the Midcap 100 1.55%, more than the Nifty 50's 0.63% gain. IT was the only sector to fall.

quiz.q: What happened in the US midterm elections, according to projections?
options: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate
quiz.why: US networks projected that Democrats won both houses of Congress, so President Trump will need their support for new laws.

quiz.q: Why do investors watch BEL's order inflow so closely?
options: It shows how much tax BEL pays
New orders become the company's future sales
It sets the price of petrol
It decides the RBI's interest rate
quiz.why: Defence companies earn money by delivering big contracts over years, so new orders today point to sales in future years.

quiz.q: Why did the rupee strengthen today?
options: Cheaper oil, a weaker dollar and foreign investors' buying
quiz.why: Easing crude prices, a weaker dollar and foreign inflows lifted the rupee 17 paise to 94.58 (provisional).

quiz.q: What did the RBI say about the viral circular on a shortage of ₹10, ₹20 and ₹50 notes?
options: Notes will be replaced by coins
quiz.why: The RBI dismissed the claim and called the circular forged, BusinessToday reported.

glossary.definition: An index of 30 large companies listed on the BSE. Its number goes up or down as their share prices change.
glossary.more: The Sensex, short for 'sensitive index', is one of India's two headline market numbers. It combines the share prices of 30 big, established companies such as banks, IT firms and Reliance, giving bigger companies more weight. It's like a class's average marks where toppers count extra: a few big names can move it a lot. When a news report says 'the market rose 400 points', it usually means the Sensex. The percentage change matters more than the points, because 400 points is a smaller share of a bigger number.

glossary.definition: An index of 50 large companies listed on the NSE, India's biggest stock exchange.
glossary.more: The Nifty 50 is the NSE's headline index and the most widely followed measure of Indian shares. It covers 50 large companies from many sectors, weighted by size. Many index funds and ETFs simply copy it, so when the Nifty rises 0.65%, a Nifty index fund rises by about the same. Think of it as a basket of India's 50 biggest shops: if the basket's total value rises, the index rises. News reports often quote it alongside the Sensex; the two usually move in the same direction.

glossary.definition: A run of consecutive days, weeks or matches in which something keeps going up or winning.
glossary.more: In market news, a winning streak means an index such as the Sensex has closed higher than the day before for several sessions in a row. Reporters count the days because long streaks are fairly rare: on most stretches, up days and down days mix. It is like a batsman scoring fifties in five matches in a row. A streak says nothing about what happens next. It can end the following day, and a long run of gains often tempts some investors to sell and lock in profits, which is called profit booking.

glossary.definition: A company of medium size by stock market value, smaller than the biggest firms but larger than small ones.
glossary.more: Indian markets group listed companies by size, measured by market value. The largest are large caps; the next tier is midcaps; then smallcaps. Midcap shares can grow faster than giants but tend to swing more. The Nifty Midcap 100 index tracks 100 such firms. Picture a town's businesses: the big mall, then busy local supermarkets, then small corner shops. Midcaps are the supermarkets. News reports often compare midcap moves with the Sensex to show whether a rally is broad or narrow.

glossary.definition: A smaller listed company by stock market value. These shares usually rise and fall more sharply.
glossary.more: Smallcaps are the smallest group of listed companies by market value. They can grow quickly, but they are also riskier: their shares can fall hard in bad times and are sometimes harder to sell. The Nifty Smallcap 100 index tracks 100 such firms. They are like small neighbourhood shops: some become big chains, many stay small, and a few close. When news reports say 'smallcaps underperformed', it means these shares did worse than the big indices that day.

glossary.definition: An index that tracks shares from one industry only, such as IT, banks or carmakers.
glossary.more: A sectoral index shows how one part of the market is doing. The Nifty IT tracks big technology companies; the Nifty Bank tracks banks; the Nifty FMCG tracks consumer-goods makers. It helps you see which industries are driving a day's move. Think of it like a school report that shows marks by subject, not just the overall total. News reports often say things like 'Nifty IT rose 3.9%, the best sector', which tells you where most of the buying happened.

glossary.definition: An NSE index that tracks the biggest listed media and entertainment companies, such as TV broadcasters and film firms.
glossary.more: The Nifty Media index follows companies that run TV channels, make and distribute films, operate cinemas and publish content, for example Zee Entertainment, Sun TV and PVR INOX. It is a small index with only a handful of companies, so a big move in one or two of them can make the whole index jump or fall sharply. Think of it like a small class of ten students: if two toppers do brilliantly, the class average rises a lot. When news says 'media shares surged 5%', it usually refers to this index.

glossary.definition: Short for real estate: companies that build and sell homes, offices and malls.
glossary.more: Realty companies such as DLF, Godrej Properties and Lodha build housing and commercial property. The Nifty Realty index tracks the listed ones. Their shares are very sensitive to interest rates, because most homebuyers take loans: when EMIs rise, fewer people buy flats. They also swing a lot because their profits arrive in lumps as projects are completed. It's like a mango seller whose income depends on one season. News reports often say 'realty stocks led the fall' on days when worries about rates or inflation rise.

glossary.definition: Shares of companies that mine or make metals like steel, aluminium, copper and zinc.
glossary.more: Metal stocks include steelmakers like Tata Steel and JSW Steel, and companies like Hindalco and Vedanta. Their profits rise and fall with global metal prices, which in turn depend on how fast economies are building roads, factories and homes. China is the world's biggest metal buyer, so news from China matters a lot. These shares often swing more than the overall market. It's like a construction labourer's income: plenty of work in boom times, lean months when building slows.

glossary.definition: An index of the biggest information technology companies listed on the NSE, such as TCS and Infosys.
glossary.more: The Nifty IT index tracks India's largest software and IT services companies, including TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra. These companies earn most of their money from clients in the US and Europe, so the index often moves on news from abroad, the dollar-rupee rate and quarterly results, rather than on Indian events. It is like a team of exporters inside the market: when foreign customers are spending, they do well. News reports mention it as one of the 'sectoral indices', for example 'Nifty IT rose 2.88%, the only sector in the green'.

glossary.definition: A number that shows how much the market expects the Nifty to swing over the next month. Higher means more nervousness.
glossary.more: India VIX is often called the 'fear gauge'. It is worked out from the prices of Nifty options, which traders buy to protect themselves or bet on big moves. When traders expect wild swings, they pay more for that protection and the VIX rises. When they feel calm, it falls. Think of it like the price of umbrellas going up before a storm is forecast. A VIX in the low teens is usually considered fairly calm. News reports quote its level and daily change, for example 'India VIX rose 1.98% to 13.88'.

glossary.definition: A tax a country charges on goods brought in from another country.
glossary.more: A tariff makes imported goods more expensive, which can protect local makers but raises prices for buyers. If the US puts a 25% tariff on Indian shirts, a $10 shirt costs American shops $12.50 at the border, so they may buy fewer of them. That hurts Indian exporters and their workers. Over the past two years, US tariff decisions have moved stock markets worldwide. When analysts say a political change could bring a 'more measured approach to tariffs', they mean fewer sudden or very large new taxes on trade.

glossary.definition: The central government's yearly plan for how it will earn and spend money, presented by the Finance Minister, usually on 1 February.
glossary.more: The Budget sets out tax rates, spending on things like roads, defence and subsidies, and how much the government will borrow. It's like a family sitting down at the start of the year to decide how much they expect to earn, what they will spend on rent, school fees and festivals, and how much they may need to borrow. Changes to income tax, capital gains tax and STT are usually announced in the Budget, which is why markets watch it closely and why talk about it starts months earlier.

glossary.definition: Foreign institutional investor: a large overseas fund that buys or sells Indian shares and bonds.
glossary.more: FIIs, also called FPIs (foreign portfolio investors), include big pension funds, mutual funds and hedge funds based abroad. Because they move large sums, their buying or selling can push the market and the rupee. When they sell Indian shares, they often convert rupees back into dollars, which can weaken the rupee. The exchanges publish provisional figures each evening, like 'FIIs sold ₹5,285.37 crore'. Think of them as big out-of-town wholesale buyers at a mandi: when they leave, prices can drop.

glossary.definition: Domestic institutional investor: a large Indian investor such as a mutual fund, insurer or pension fund.
glossary.more: DIIs include Indian mutual funds, LIC and other insurers, banks and pension funds like the EPFO. Much of their money comes from ordinary Indians through SIPs and insurance premiums. In recent years, DIIs have often bought when foreign investors sold, cushioning the market. It's like local buyers stepping in at a mandi when out-of-town traders leave. News reports usually show FII and DII figures side by side each evening, for example 'DIIs bought ₹3,319.39 crore'.

glossary.definition: An early figure that may be revised slightly once final data comes in.
glossary.more: Many market figures are first reported as provisional, meaning early and subject to change. The rupee's closing rate is often reported provisionally right at the close and then confirmed later, and the daily FII and DII buying and selling figures are provisional too. For example, Thursday's rupee close was first reported as 94.82 but finally came in at 94.81. It's like an exam's provisional result before re-checking. The changes are usually small, but they do happen, which is why reports often add '(provisional)' after a number.

glossary.definition: A Systematic Investment Plan: investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals, usually monthly.
glossary.more: An SIP lets you invest a set sum, say ₹2,000, into a mutual fund automatically every month. It's like a recurring deposit, but the money goes into a fund whose value rises and falls with the market. Because you invest the same amount every month, you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when prices are high. Millions of Indians invest this way, and the total monthly SIP inflow is reported regularly in the news. Those flows are a big reason domestic funds have been steady buyers of shares.

glossary.definition: US national elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, mainly for seats in Congress.
glossary.more: In the US, the president is elected every four years, but elections for the whole House of Representatives and about a third of the Senate happen every two years. The ones that fall in the middle of a president's term are called midterms; this year they are on 3 November. The results decide which party controls Congress, which can make it easier or harder for the president to pass laws. It's a bit like a mid-term vote on a housing society committee that can change who controls the budget. Markets watch them because policy on taxes, trade and war can shift afterwards.

glossary.definition: When one party holds the presidency and another controls the parliament, so neither can easily pass laws alone.
glossary.more: In the US, the President comes from one party, but laws must pass through Congress, made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate. If the other party controls Congress, the President needs its agreement for new laws and budgets. This often leads to gridlock: fewer big changes, slower decisions. Markets sometimes like this, because it lowers the chance of sudden, sweeping policy shifts, and can limit government borrowing. Think of a family where a big purchase needs both parents' agreement: fewer impulse buys, but also slower decisions.

glossary.definition: Contracts that let traders bet on where a share index will be later. Before a market opens, their prices hint at how it may start.
glossary.more: Futures are agreements to buy or sell something at a set price on a future date. Index futures, such as those on the US S&P 500 or Dow Jones, trade almost round the clock. Because the US stock market opens only in the Indian evening, Indian news often reports 'US futures were down 0.5%' during our trading day. That's an early signal of how American investors are feeling. It's like checking the queue outside a shop before it opens to guess how busy the day will be.

glossary.definition: A US stock index of 30 large American companies, one of the world's most watched market numbers.
glossary.more: The Dow Jones Industrial Average, usually just 'the Dow', tracks 30 big US companies such as Apple, JPMorgan and Coca-Cola. It is one of the oldest stock indices in the world. Indian news reports mention it because what happens on Wall Street overnight often sets the mood for Asian and Indian markets the next morning. It is like checking the weather in a big neighbouring city before you step out. The S&P 500, which covers 500 companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq are the other two US indices you will often see quoted.

glossary.definition: The interest rate the US government pays on its bonds. It affects borrowing costs worldwide.
glossary.more: US Treasury bonds are loans to the US government. The yield is the return investors earn on them. Because these bonds are seen as very safe, their yields set a baseline for interest rates around the world. When US yields rise, global investors may pull money from riskier places like India; when they fall, India can look more attractive. It's like a bank's FD rate rising: people move savings from riskier options into the safe deposit.

glossary.definition: One-hundredth of one percentage point. 100 basis points equal 1 percentage point.
glossary.more: Basis points are used to describe small changes in interest rates and bond yields precisely. If a yield falls from 5.19% to 5.085%, that is a drop of 10.5 basis points. Saying '10.5 basis points' avoids confusion between a change in percentage points and a percentage change. It's like measuring medicine in millilitres instead of spoonfuls: more exact for small amounts. News about RBI rate decisions often uses basis points too, as in a '25 basis point' cut or hike.

glossary.definition: A measure of the US dollar's value against six major currencies, such as the euro and yen.
glossary.more: The dollar index, often called DXY, shows whether the US dollar is getting stronger or weaker against a basket of major currencies. When it rises, currencies like the rupee usually weaken; when it falls, they often gain. It's like a thermometer for the dollar's strength worldwide. Forex reports in India often mention it alongside the rupee's close, because it helps separate two questions: is the rupee weak because of India-specific reasons such as oil, or simply because the dollar is strong against everyone?

glossary.definition: The price of gold for immediate delivery in global markets, quoted in US dollars per ounce.
glossary.more: Spot gold is the international price at which gold changes hands right now, unlike futures, which are deals for a later date. It is quoted in US dollars per troy ounce, about 31.1 grams. Indian prices, such as those on MCX, follow spot gold closely but also depend on the rupee-dollar exchange rate and import duties. So if spot gold rises and the rupee weakens on the same day, Indian gold gets doubly expensive. Jewellers' shop prices then add GST and making charges on top.

glossary.definition: The Multi Commodity Exchange of India, where gold, silver, oil and other commodities are traded.
glossary.more: MCX is India's main exchange for trading commodities such as gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas and metals. Most trading is in futures contracts, which are agreements on a price for a future date. MCX gold prices are a common guide to what jewellers charge, though shop prices also include GST and making charges. It's like a big wholesale mandi for metals and energy. News reports quote MCX gold per 10 grams.

glossary.definition: A Hindu festival two days before Diwali when many families traditionally buy gold, silver, utensils or vehicles.
glossary.more: Dhanteras marks the start of the Diwali festivities in much of India. Buying something made of metal on this day is considered lucky, so jewellers see some of their biggest sales of the year. That is why news about gold in October and November often mentions Dhanteras demand, and why a price fall just before the festival is closely watched: shoppers may buy more, or buy heavier pieces, if prices dip. Carmakers and two-wheeler makers also report a rush of bookings and deliveries around this time.

glossary.definition: Companies that write software, run computer systems and provide tech support for clients, mostly abroad.
glossary.more: India's IT services firms, such as TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Tech Mahindra, do technology work for banks, shops, airlines and governments around the world. Most of their revenue comes in dollars or euros, while most of their staff are paid in rupees. So a weaker rupee usually helps their profits. It's like a tailor in Tiruppur stitching for foreign buyers: paid in dollars, spending in rupees. IT firms are big parts of the Sensex and Nifty, so their results can move the whole market.

glossary.definition: A country whose economy and financial markets are growing but not yet considered fully developed.
glossary.more: Emerging markets include countries like India, China, Brazil and Indonesia. Their economies often grow faster than rich countries, but their markets can be riskier and swing more. Global funds often have a set amount for 'emerging markets', so being in that group brings steady foreign investment. Losing that status can mean big outflows, as Indonesia feared on Friday. It's like a school being listed among 'top schools' in a guide; parents pay more attention to those.

glossary.definition: Shares of companies that make weapons, radars, ships, aircraft or electronics for the armed forces.
glossary.more: In India, many defence companies are government-owned, such as Bharat Electronics (BEL), Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL) and Mazagon Dock. Their main customer is the Ministry of Defence, so their business depends on government orders, which come in large contracts that take years to deliver. Investors watch the size of these orders closely. Defence shares often rise when the government announces bigger defence budgets or a push to make more equipment in India. Like a contractor with a few huge clients, one big order, or a delay, can move the share price sharply.

glossary.definition: A company's report of its earnings, costs and profit for a three-month period.
glossary.more: Listed companies in India must publish results every quarter: April–June, July–September, October–December and January–March. These show revenue, expenses and profit, usually compared with the same quarter a year earlier and the previous quarter. Investors use them to judge whether a business is improving. It's like a student's term report card, which parents read closely. 'Results season' is the few weeks when most companies report, and individual share prices can jump or fall sharply on the day.

glossary.definition: The profit of a company together with its subsidiaries, such as a bank plus its insurance or broking arms.
glossary.more: Many Indian companies own other companies. ICICI Bank, for example, owns stakes in insurance, broking and fund businesses. Standalone profit covers only the main company; consolidated profit adds up the whole group. It's like the income of one earning member versus the income of the whole joint family. The two figures can grow at different rates, which is why news reports sometimes quote different percentages for the same results. When comparing numbers, check which basis is being used.

glossary.definition: A comparison with the same period one year earlier.
glossary.more: Year-on-year, often written YoY, compares a figure with the same period last year, such as July–September 2026 against July–September 2025. This removes seasonal effects: many businesses naturally earn more in festive months, so comparing with the previous quarter can mislead. It's like comparing this Diwali's sweet-shop sales with last Diwali's, not with a quiet month. Company results, inflation and GDP are usually reported year-on-year.

glossary.definition: The total money a company earns from selling its goods or services, before costs are taken out.
glossary.more: Revenue is the top line of a company's results: everything it billed customers in a period. Profit is what's left after paying for materials, salaries, interest, taxes and other costs. A tea stall that sells ₹10,000 of tea in a day has ₹10,000 of revenue, but its profit might be only ₹2,000 after milk, sugar, gas and rent. Revenue can rise while profit falls, if costs rise faster. That's why news reports on results usually quote both, often with the change from a year earlier.

glossary.definition: The total value of work a company has signed contracts for but not yet completed.
glossary.more: An order book is the pile of pending work a company has already won. New orders add to it; finished work moves out of it and becomes revenue. A tailor with 200 unstitched orders waiting has a bigger order book than one with 20, and can be surer of income in coming months. For companies like L&T, the order book is often several times a year's revenue, which gives investors visibility into future earnings. News reports quote it as a figure in crore or lakh crore at the end of a quarter.

glossary.definition: The value of new contracts a company wins in a period, such as a quarter.
glossary.more: For engineering and construction companies like L&T, order inflow is the value of new projects signed in a period: metro lines, power plants, factories and so on. It's like a tailor counting how many new stitching orders came into the shop this month. The money is earned later, as the work is done, so strong order inflow today usually points to more revenue in future years. Results reports for such companies often lead with order inflow alongside profit, and a record figure is treated as a sign of strong demand.

glossary.definition: A company's own forecast for its future sales or profit growth.
glossary.more: Many companies, especially IT firms, tell investors roughly how much they expect to grow over the year, for example 'revenue growth of 2.5% to 4%'. This is called guidance. Investors watch it closely because it shows how confident the management is. If a company raises guidance, it signals business is better than expected; if it cuts guidance, shares often fall even when the latest quarter looks good. It's like a shopkeeper telling a lender how much sales they expect this Diwali season. Guidance is a forecast, not a promise.

glossary.definition: The price an analyst expects a share to reach, usually within about a year.
glossary.more: Brokerage firms study companies and publish a target price along with a rating like 'buy', 'outperform' or 'sell'. A target is an educated guess, not a promise, and analysts often change targets as news changes. Different firms can have very different targets for the same share. It's like a weather forecast: useful to know, but it can be wrong. News reports quote target prices often, for example 'Macquarie sees the stock reaching ₹1,965'. Market Primer reports these views but never recommends buying or selling.

glossary.definition: A firm that buys and sells shares for clients and publishes research and forecasts on companies.
glossary.more: Brokerages such as Jefferies, Nomura or Motilal Oswal do two jobs. They carry out trades for investors, and their analysts study companies and publish reports with forecasts and views. When news reports say 'Jefferies expected sales of 585,000 units', they are quoting one of these forecasts. Brokerage forecasts are educated guesses, not guarantees, and different brokerages often disagree. For an ordinary reader, it helps to think of them as expert commentators, like cricket analysts predicting a score before an innings.

glossary.definition: The lowest price a share or index has traded at over the past year.
glossary.more: The 52-week low is the cheapest a share has been in the last 52 weeks, or one year. Its opposite is the 52-week high. News reports mention it because touching a one-year low often signals that investors have become pessimistic about a company or industry. But cheap doesn't automatically mean good value: a share can keep falling after hitting a 52-week low. Think of it like the lowest price you've seen for onions all year; it tells you where prices are, not where they will go next.

glossary.definition: The price of one currency in terms of another, such as how many rupees buy one US dollar.
glossary.more: The exchange rate tells you how much of your currency you need to buy foreign money. At 94.92, one US dollar costs ₹94.92. If it moves to 94.50, the rupee has strengthened; if to 95.50, it has weakened. The rate affects the cost of imports like oil and electronics, foreign travel and studying abroad, and the earnings of exporters. It's like the price of onions at the mandi: it changes daily with supply and demand. News reports quote it most evenings.

glossary.definition: One-hundredth of a rupee. Rupee moves against the dollar are usually reported in paise.
glossary.more: There are 100 paise in a rupee. When reports say 'the rupee rose 7 paise to 94.92', it means one dollar now costs ₹94.92 instead of ₹94.99. A few paise sounds tiny, but on large sums it adds up: on $1 million, 7 paise is ₹70,000. That's why importers, exporters and the RBI follow these small moves closely. Think of it like a small rise in the price of petrol per litre; small per unit, big across millions of litres.

glossary.definition: A widely used international benchmark price for crude oil.
glossary.more: Brent crude is a type of oil originally from the North Sea, and its price is used as a reference for much of the world's oil trade. India imports most of its crude oil, so a higher Brent price raises India's import bill, can weaken the rupee and can push up fuel and transport costs. Think of it like the wholesale price of wheat that sets what bakeries pay. News reports quote Brent in dollars per barrel, like '$105.56 a barrel'.

glossary.definition: The standard unit for measuring oil, equal to about 159 litres.
glossary.more: Oil prices are quoted per barrel, a unit equal to about 159 litres. When Brent is $105 a barrel, that is roughly $0.66 per litre of crude, before refining, transport, taxes and dealer margins. So petrol at the pump costs far more than crude per litre. It's a bit like quoting rice prices per quintal at a wholesale market, even though you buy a few kilos at the shop. News reports always use 'per barrel' for crude oil prices.

glossary.definition: The total amount a country pays to buy goods from other countries over a period.
glossary.more: India buys most of its crude oil, plus gold, electronics and more, from abroad, and pays in dollars. The import bill is the total of those payments. When oil prices rise, the import bill swells even if India buys the same number of barrels. It is like a household's grocery bill going up because the price of cooking oil jumped, not because the family ate more. A bigger import bill means more demand for dollars, which tends to weaken the rupee, and it can push up prices at home.

glossary.definition: The Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank. It sets interest rates, regulates banks and manages the rupee.
glossary.more: The RBI is like the bank of all banks. It decides the repo rate, the interest rate at which banks borrow from it, which shapes the rates on your home loan EMI and fixed deposit. It also supervises banks, prints currency notes, manages India's foreign exchange reserves and steps in when the rupee moves too sharply. It runs markets for government bonds and money markets too. When the RBI changes a rule, it usually issues a circular on its website, so a 'circular' shared on WhatsApp should be checked there.

glossary.definition: The Securities and Exchange Board of India, the regulator that oversees the stock market.
glossary.more: SEBI makes and enforces the rules for stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, listed companies and IPOs. Its job is to protect investors and keep markets fair. It can fine companies, ban traders and change how trading works, like Friday's new closing-auction rules. Think of it as the umpire in a cricket match: it doesn't play, but it makes sure everyone follows the rules. SEBI announcements usually come as circulars or board-meeting decisions.

glossary.definition: The market where banks, companies and the government borrow and lend money for short periods, from one day up to a year.
glossary.more: Banks often need cash for just a night or a few weeks, to cover withdrawals or meet RBI rules. They borrow it from other banks or investors in the money market, through instruments like call money loans, treasury bills and certificates of deposit. Interest rates here move closely with the RBI's repo rate. Ordinary savers touch this market through liquid and money market mutual funds. Think of it as a short-term lending window: like borrowing ₹500 from a friend until payday, but in crores and between institutions.

glossary.definition: Bonds and bills issued by the central or state governments to borrow money, also called G-secs.
glossary.more: When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows by selling government securities. Buyers lend money and get regular interest and their money back on a set date. Short-term ones, under a year, are treasury bills; longer ones are dated bonds, some lasting 30 or 40 years. Banks, insurers, pension funds and mutual funds are the biggest buyers, but individuals can also buy them through the RBI's Retail Direct portal. Their yields act as a base for many other interest rates in India, including loan rates.

glossary.definition: The market where currencies are bought and sold, such as rupees for dollars.
glossary.more: The foreign exchange, or forex, market is where banks, companies, investors and the RBI swap one currency for another. An oil importer needs dollars to pay for crude, so it buys dollars with rupees. A foreign investor buying Indian shares does the opposite. These deals set the exchange rate you see in the news, such as 94.58 rupees per dollar. For you, it shows up when you pay for a foreign trip, an overseas course or an imported phone. The RBI oversees India's forex market and sometimes trades in it to smooth sharp moves.

glossary.definition: Contracts, such as futures and options, whose value depends on the price of something else.
glossary.more: A derivative is a contract based on an underlying asset, like a share, an index or gold. Futures are agreements to buy or sell at a set price on a future date; options give the right, but not the obligation, to do so. They are used to protect against price swings, and also for speculation. SEBI has warned that most individual traders lose money in futures and options. It's like booking a wedding hall's price today for a date months away.
